# RecreationPrompt.md

Create a mobile-first one-screen physics puzzle called **Hogwarts Spell Drop**. The game should preserve a Cut-the-Rope-style core loop: a magical treat hangs from one or more rope-like enchanted bindings, and the player swipes across the screen like casting a wand slash to cut those bindings. The treat must swing and fall under gravity into a magical target at the bottom of the screen. Optional glowing house-point sigils can be collected along the path for bonus score. Reaching the target wins; falling out of bounds loses; restarting immediately creates another playable puzzle.

Use a Harry Potter-inspired wizard-school presentation without changing the core mechanics. The treat can look like a Golden Snitch candy, chocolate frog sweet, or glowing charm. The ropes should appear as luminous spell bindings. The swipe trail should look like a bright wand slash with sparks. The target should be a friendly magical recipient such as the Sorting Hat, a hungry spellbook, a cauldron, or a magical creature. The HUD should read as parchment-and-ink house points, with clear touch-safe overlays and large mobile-readable buttons.

Plan the experience as a five-stage Hogwarts journey: classroom charm practice, moving staircase corridor, Quidditch pitch, Forbidden Forest, and Great Hall finale. Each stage should feel visually distinct through procedural backgrounds, palette, floating candles, house banners, castle silhouettes, mist, and spell particles, while preserving the same input, physics, scoring, and win/loss rules. Difficulty may escalate only through safe existing puzzle dimensions such as rope count, spacing, collectible placement, and timing pressure if those knobs are already stable. Do not add character movement, combat, inventory, dialogue trees, or RPG systems. The signature interaction remains: swipe to cut magical bindings, watch the object swing, collect sigils, and feed the target.\n

# Blueprint.md — Remix Inference Plus

## Current game reality

### High-level code structure
- `index.html` is the complete canonical game surface.
- CSS defines a candy-themed one-screen presentation, mobile-safe overlays, HUD, start screen, game-over screen, feedback GIF placement, and canvas sizing.
- Inline JavaScript contains:
  - `AudioManager` for BGM/SFX loading, unlock, fallback synthesis, and visibility pause.
  - `VPoint` and `VStick` as the protected Verlet physics primitives.
  - `Game` as the state machine, input handler, level generator, update loop, collision/progress checker, and canvas renderer.
- No external gameplay JS files are present. Catalog files exist only for approved future media selection.

### Game loop / state model
- States: `START`, `PLAYING`, `GAMEOVER`, `WIN`.
- On load, a demo rope/candy simulation is created behind the start overlay.
- Any pointer down on the start screen starts play unless the restart button is the event target.
- During play, pointer drag creates a swipe trail and cuts active rope segments when the swipe line intersects a rope segment.
- The candy is simulated through Verlet movement and rope constraints every animation frame.
- The round ends in win when the candy reaches the target mouth and in failure when the candy leaves the screen bounds.
- After end state, a modal appears with score and restart.

### Player goals
- Primary goal: cut ropes in the right sequence/timing so the candy falls into the target mouth.
- Secondary score goal: route the candy through up to three collectible stars before feeding the target.

### Interaction pattern
- Mobile-first pointer swipe.
- Press/drag to cut ropes; release clears trail.
- Tap start/restart to begin another randomized one-screen puzzle.

### Core systems
- Rope/candy physics using points and stick constraints.
- Rope cutting by segment intersection.
- Procedural level setup with randomized rope count, peg positions, target location, and star positions.
- Score accumulation from star collection only.
- Win/fail detection.
- Canvas procedural drawing for candy, ropes, pegs, stars, target character, particles, background, and swipe trail.
- Audio and small reaction media feedback.

### Inferred genre/gameplay shape
- One-screen physics puzzle / Cut-the-Rope-style arcade puzzle.
- Light timing and spatial prediction.
- Single-round randomized puzzle rather than an explicit multi-level campaign.

### Current identity summary
- Current title: **Candy Drop**.
- Current theme: cheerful candy clouds and a cute monster mouth.
- Current affordance: candy on ropes, stars as treats, monster mouth as target.

## Intended Harry Potter remixed trajectory

### Remix-direction summary
Transform the presentation into a Hogwarts spellcraft rope-cutting puzzle while preserving the exact core mechanic. The candy becomes an enchanted wizarding treat or Golden Snitch-like sweet, ropes become magical threads/webs/levitation charms, the swipe becomes a wand slash spell, stars become house points or glowing spell sigils, and the target monster mouth becomes a magical recipient such as the Sorting Hat, a hungry spellbook, a cauldron, or a friendly creature.

### Preserve-vs-change guidance
#### Preserve
- Pointer/touch input semantics: swipe to cut line segments.
- Verlet physics model, gravity, friction, rope stiffness behavior, and constraint solving.
- Rope segment intersection logic.
- Randomized one-screen puzzle setup unless later stages create safe variants via existing knobs.
- Star scoring semantics: each collectible adds 100.
- Win condition: candy/treat reaches the target radius.
- Loss condition: candy/treat leaves bounds.
- Start/restart flow and mobile-safe HUD positioning.

#### Change safely
- Title, HUD labels, button text, and result copy.
- Canvas art for candy, ropes, pegs, stars, target, particles, and background.
- CSS palette, fonts, overlays, decorative DOM effects.
- Audio mapping if using approved catalog URLs, while keeping unlock/fallback behavior.
- Feedback copy and theming.
- Conceptual level names and visual evolution plan.

#### Avoid
- Rewriting the game loop, physics engine, input/collision model, win/loss scoring, or randomized setup.
- Adding inventory, combat, spell selection, character movement, or menu-heavy RPG systems.
- Making later difficulty depend on physically harder mobile gestures.\n
